prompt: Your client, a large US pharmaceutical company, has invented a prescription pill that regrows hair to teenage thickness within three months, taken daily to maintain. Estimate the US market size, then decide what price to sell it at.

clarifying.answer: It is a prescription drug, so access is gated by a doctor, not bought off the shelf.
Unisex, but it causes minor, non-permanent sexual dysfunction in 2% and can cause birth defects, so women who may have children (conservatively, all women under 40) should not take it.
The goal is to maximize profit (not share capture or a fixed payback), which shapes the pricing choice.
The pill costs $1 to make; fixed costs (R&D) are negligible for this case.

facts.note: Competitors A and B split the market evenly, similar on effectiveness, brand and accessibility. B is priced higher but sells as much (no side effects, shampoo-based, which customers mildly prefer). The client's pill is more effective and faster than both, with only minor side effects.

exhibits.title: Competitor Products (3-month course)
exhibits.unlock_condition: Candidate benchmarks against competitors and asks for their prices and product characteristics.
exhibits.so_what: A charges $450 and B charges $540; both are only standard in effectiveness. The client's pill is more effective and faster, so it can price at least at A's $450 and still undercut B's $540, letting effectiveness plus a lower total price win share.

phases.name: opening
phases.interviewer_instructions: State the prompt. Note the pricing goal (maximize profit) only if asked. Wait for the candidate to plan sizing then pricing.

coaching.explain: A pricing case should first pin the goal (maximize profit here, not share or payback) because it changes the answer. A strong candidate plans to size the market, then price via cost, competitor and value lenses.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Restate: 'I'll first size the US market of people who need and can access the cure, then price it using cost, competitor and value-to-customer lenses, aiming to maximize profit.'

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate fixes the pricing goal and plans to size then price via multiple lenses.

phases.name: market-sizing
phases.interviewer_instructions: Guide the candidate to filter the US population to balding people who would treat it and can access a prescription, excluding women under 40 (birth-defect risk). Accept an intermediate market size; note affordability depends on the yet-to-be-set price.

coaching.explain: Size the market by filtering to people with meaningful balding who would seek treatment and can get a prescription, excluding women under 40 for safety. Affordability is left open because it depends on the price still to be set. The minor 2% side effect will not deter balding men who want the cure.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Filter US population to balding adults who would treat it and can access a doctor, exclude women under 40, and leave the affordability filter until the price is set.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate builds a filtered market size (excluding women under 40) and defers the affordability filter until pricing.

phases.name: pricing-analysis
phases.interviewer_instructions: Release ex1_competitor_pricing when the candidate benchmarks competitors. Guide them through cost floor ($1 x 90 = $90), competitor benchmark (price at least A's $450, still under B's $540), and a value range. Verdicts on numbers come from the math checker.

coaching.explain: Triangulate three lenses. Cost floor: $1 x 90 days = $90, the minimum. Competitor: the client beats A on every count, so price at least A's $450 (= $150/month) and it still undercuts B's $540. Value: bracket the price with comparables, e.g. a lower cap like Starbucks coffee for three months (~$270) and an upper cap like dental braces. The three lenses converge on a band well above cost.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Set the $90 cost floor, price at A's $450 course ($150/month) since the client is superior yet still under B's $540, and sanity-check against value comparables.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate sets the cost floor, benchmarks to competitors to reach ~$150/month, and brackets it with value comparables.

phases.name: synthesis
phases.interviewer_instructions: Ask for the price recommendation and the reasoning. Look for ~$150/month with penetrate-then-raise logic, the profit per month, and awareness that the reasoning matters more than the exact figure.

coaching.explain: Recommend about $150/month: it matches A's course price while beating both rivals on effectiveness and undercutting B's total, so it wins share, and it earns a healthy $120/month over the $30 monthly cost. Start competitive to gain share, then raise price once positive reviews build. The exact number matters less than this reasoning.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: 'Price at ~$150/month ($450/course): superior to both rivals yet cheaper than B, earning ~$120/month margin. Enter competitively to capture share, then raise price as reviews build. Risk: if share is slow, we can drop toward $100/month, since cost is only $30.'

phases.pass_criteria: Recommendation lands near $150/month with penetrate-then-raise logic and the margin quantified.

common_errors: Using a monthly rather than a 3-month course for the cost floor
Forgetting the pill is taken daily
Dividing by 90 days instead of 3 months when a monthly price is wanted
Using the 3-month cost against a 1-month price
Assuming the client must match B's higher price rather than undercut it
Using a monthly coffee spend rather than the full 3-month comparable for the value lower-cap

curveballs.injected_fact: Suppose a generic competitor is expected to launch a similar pill in a year. Does your pricing change? (Strong answer: harvest the monopoly window with a higher price now, or price to build loyalty and brand before the generic arrives, depending on how sticky prescriptions are.)

model_answer.framework: Size the market by filtering the population to people who need, would take, can access and can afford the cure, then price by triangulating cost-based (floor), competitor-based (market anchor) and value-based (ceiling), against a profit-maximising goal.
key_insights: The cost floor is just $1 x 90 = $90 per course, far below what customers will pay, so cost-plus badly underprices.
The client beats competitor A on every dimension, so it can price at least A's $450 course ($150/month) and still undercut B's $540.
Value comparables (coffee as a lower cap, braces as an upper cap) confirm a price band well above cost.
At $150/month the margin is $120, leaving room to drop toward $100 to accelerate share if needed.
model_answer.recommendation: Price at about $150/month ($450 per course): superior to both rivals yet cheaper than B, so it wins share while earning ~$120/month margin. Launch competitively to build share and reviews, then raise price as the product's reputation grows. If share is slow, there is room to cut toward $100/month given the trivial $30 monthly cost.
model_answer.walkthrough: Fix the profit-maximising goal, size the filtered market (excluding women under 40), set the $90 cost floor, benchmark to competitors for a ~$150/month anchor, bracket with value comparables, and recommend a penetrate-then-raise price.

anchors.1: No structure; picks a price with no lenses or sizing.
anchors.3: Uses one pricing lens or sizes without pricing method.
anchors.5: Sizes the filtered market and prices via cost, competitor and value lenses toward the stated goal.

anchors.1: Cannot compute the cost floor or convert a course price to monthly.
anchors.3: Computes the floor but not the margin or the value comparables.
anchors.5: Computes the $90 floor, the $150/month anchor, and the $120 margin cleanly.

anchors.1: Defaults to cost-plus despite value far exceeding cost.
anchors.3: Benchmarks competitors but ignores the client's superiority or the value ceiling.
anchors.5: Prices off the client's superiority versus rivals and confirms with a value range.

anchors.1: Rambling or silent; cannot justify the price.
anchors.3: States a price but does not narrate the three-lens reasoning.
anchors.5: Clearly narrates cost, competitor and value reasoning and why the number follows.

anchors.1: No price, or a number with no reasoning.
anchors.3: Gives a price but omits the penetrate-then-raise logic or the margin.
anchors.5: Recommends ~$150/month with penetrate-then-raise logic, the margin, and a risk.
